generated.title: We're Triggering Earthquakes. And We Know How. #shorts
generated.description:
Humans can trigger real earthquakes, and oil and gas operations are part of the story. But it usually isn't the drilling.

The main culprit in the central United States is deep wastewater disposal. Oil and gas production brings up huge volumes of salty wastewater, and companies pump it into deep rock layers. That can raise fluid pressure on faults already under natural stress, and sometimes those faults slip.

Drilling, fracking and wastewater injection are different things. Drilling makes the well. Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) briefly injects fluid to crack shale, and USGS ties only 1-2% of Oklahoma's earthquakes to it. Disposal wells run for much longer and inject far more fluid. Even so, most injection wells are not linked to felt earthquakes.

On September 3, 2016, a magnitude 5.8 earthquake struck about 14 km northwest of Pawnee, Oklahoma, the state's largest on record. It ruptured a previously unmapped fault. Researchers linked the sequence to wastewater injection: one study says it "appears to have been induced" by high-volume disposal within 10 km, while others describe an interplay of injection, tectonic faults and foreshocks, and the exact role is still studied. Humans don't move tectonic plates, and injection doesn't create these faults.

Sources:
- USGS event us10006jxs: https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us10006jxs
- USGS, Myths and Misconceptions About Induced Earthquakes: https://www.usgs.gov/programs/earthquake-hazards/myths-and-misconceptions-about-induced-earthquakes
- McGarr & Barbour (2017), "Wastewater Disposal and the Earthquake Sequences During 2016 Near Fairview, Pawnee, and Cushing, Oklahoma", Geophysical Research Letters: https://doi.org/10.1002/2017GL075258
- Yeck et al. (2017), "Oklahoma experiences largest earthquake during ongoing regional wastewater injection hazard mitigation efforts", Geophysical Research Letters: https://doi.org/10.1002/2016GL071685
- Chen et al. (2017), "The Pawnee earthquake as a result of the interplay among injection, faults and foreshocks", Scientific Reports: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-04992-z
- Barbour, Norbeck & Rubinstein (2017), "The Effects of Varying Injection Rates in Osage County, Oklahoma, on the 2016 Mw 5.8 Pawnee Earthquake", Seismological Research Letters: https://doi.org/10.1785/0220170003

Visuals are AI-generated illustrations; the underground scenes are schematic and not to scale. They are not photographs or footage of the 2016 earthquake, and the plains landscape is not Pawnee. The epicenter map uses USGS data.
